question: How do they measure style transfer success?
title: Grammatical Error Correction and Style Transfer via Zero-shot Monolingual Translation
answer_short: They measure style transfer success by calculating the root mean square error (RMSE) between human evaluator scores and desired style direction values, where +1 indicates more formal and -1 more informal.
answer_rationale: Text 4 explicitly describes the evaluation method: human evaluators assign scores (+1, -1, or 0) based on style direction, and RMSE is calculated between these scores and desired values. Text 3 and Text 7 provide supporting context on human evaluation and agreement rates, reinforcing that human evaluators are central to measuring success. Text 6 confirms that qualitative and quantitative manual evaluation is part of the methodology.

question: Do they introduce errors in the data or does the data already contain them?

extractive_spans: all three languages have error-corrected corpora for testing purposes
evidence: We use three languages in our experiments: English, Estonian and Latvian. All three have different characteristics, for example Latvian and (especially) Estonian are morphologically complex and have loose word order, while English has a strict word order and the morphology is much simpler. Most importantly, all three languages have error-corrected corpora for testing purposes, though work on their automatic grammatical error correction is extremely limited (see Section SECREF3 ).
We use the following error-corrected corpora both for scoring and as basis for manual analysis:
for English: CoNLL-2014 BIBREF5 and JFLEG BIBREF20 corpora
for Estonian: the Learner Language Corpus BIBREF21
for Latvian: the Error-annotated Corpus of Latvian BIBREF22
All of these are based on language learner (L2) essays and their manual corrections.

title: Grammatical Error Correction and Style Transfer via Zero-shot Monolingual Translation
answer_rationale: Text 10 states that 'Not all English sentences included errors. 30 sentences remained unchanged, out of which 17 had no mistakes in them.' This indicates that the data already contain errors, as some sentences were erroneous and required correction, while others were error-free. The model corrects errors present in the data, implying the errors were not introduced by the model but were already in the data.

question: What error types is their model more reliable for?

extractive_spans: grammatical, spelling and word order errors
evidence: To conclude this section, our model reliable corrects grammatical, spelling and word order errors on , with more mixed performance on lexical choice errors and some unnecessary paraphrasing of the input. The error types that the model manages well can be traced back to having a strong monolingual language model, a common trait of a good NMT model. As the model operates on the level of word parts and its vocabulary is limited, this leads to combining wrong word parts, sometimes across languages. This could be fixed by either using character-based NMT or doing automatic spelling correction prior to applying our current model.

extractive_spans: spelling, word order and grammatical errors
evidence: We showed that for GEC our approach reliably corrects spelling, word order and grammatical errors, while being less reliable on lexical choice errors. Applied to style transfer our model is very good at meaning preservation and output fluency, while reliably transferring style for English contractions, lexical choice and grammatical constructions. The main benefit is that no annotated data is used to train the model, thus making it very easy to train it for other (especially under-resourced) languages.

title: Grammatical Error Correction and Style Transfer via Zero-shot Monolingual Translation
answer_short: grammatical, spelling and word order errors
answer_rationale: Text 7 states: 'our model reliable corrects grammatical, spelling and word order errors'. This directly identifies the error types the model is more reliable for.

question: How does their parallel data differ in terms of style?
title: Grammatical Error Correction and Style Transfer via Zero-shot Monolingual Translation
answer_short: OpenSubtitles2018 is more informal, Europarl and JRC-Acquis are more formal.
answer_rationale: Text 3 states that OpenSubtitles2018 is comprised of movie and TV subtitles, which are assumed to be more informal, while Europarl and JRC-Acquis are proceedings and documents of the European Parliament, assumed to be more formal. Text 1 reinforces this by stating that movie subtitles gravitate towards the more informal style, and parliament proceedings towards the more formal style.
